title: Party links and bribery claims taint new fertiliser dealerships
excerpt: Party leaders' relatives won dealerships in several districts before the Boro season, a Daily Star probe found. The minister promises an inquiry.
content:
People linked to the ruling BNP, including relatives of local leaders and an MP, won many of the government's new fertiliser dealerships, often with little trading experience, The Daily Star reported on 14 November, from reporting in Rangpur, Rajshahi, Kushtia, Jhenaidah, Thakurgaon and Brahmanbaria.

What the reporting found

  • Scale: more than 47,000 applications for about 5,000 posts; 4,503 dealerships awarded and 238 pending, according to agriculture ministry figures.
  • Kushtia: at least 50 of 70 dealerships went to BNP-linked people or relatives.
  • Thakurgaon: 28 of 31 new dealers were reportedly BNP leaders, activists, relatives or associates.
  • Jhenaidah: about 90% of new dealers had no previous fertiliser business.
  • Rangpur division: unsuccessful applicants alleged bribes of up to Tk 20 lakh for a dealership. Those named denied any payments.

The rules require dealers to live in the area and have a warehouse holding at least 50 tonnes. In Brahmanbaria, the newspaper found an abandoned rice mill listed as the warehouse for an MP's son's dealership. The MP disputed this.

Agriculture Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid said the government used a multi-level verification process. "All complaints will be investigated and officials responsible for improper verification will be held accountable," he told the newspaper. Agricultural economist Jahangir Alam Khan warned that unsuitable dealers could worsen shortages and threaten food security, and called for a fresh investigation.

The supply picture

Bangladesh needs about 58 lakh tonnes of fertiliser a year but can make only 12 lakh tonnes, so it must import more than 46 lakh tonnes this year. The FY27 fertiliser subsidy is Tk 17,000 crore, down from Tk 28,987 crore the year before, the report said. Shortages have already been reported in several districts ahead of the Boro rice season (January to June).

Why it matters

Dealers are the last link between subsidised fertiliser and small farmers. If dealerships go to people without stores or experience, small and tenant farmers, who are least able to pay black-market prices, are hit first. NGOs running farmer groups and food security programmes may want to track supply and prices in their areas and report problems to upazila agriculture offices.

What to watch

Whether the ministry opens the promised investigation, cancels any dealerships, and how fertiliser supplies hold up when Boro planting begins.

Sources

  • Party ties, family links, 'bribery' taint fertiliser dealership, The Daily Star, 14 November 2026
